title: Open a hanging locker padlock by its dial: right past two turns, left one turn past, right to the third, then pull
instruction: Open the padlock on the locker with the combination 24-8-31, and leave it hanging open on the locker's hasp.
context: Opening a dial combination padlock on a school, gym or workplace locker is something most adults have done many times. The maker's directions: turn the dial right three times and stop on the first number, turn left one full turn past the first number and stop on the second, turn right and stop on the third, then pull. The lock hangs free from the hasp, so the hand that turns the 33 mm dial also drags the body, which swings and twists as the dial turns; numbers are read against the body's index mark. Each number has to stop on its mark at the index, within half a mark (4.5 degrees, so the index reads that number and not a neighbour), after several turns made by letting go and re-gripping, with two reversals: overshoot a number or reverse wrongly and the wheel pack is no longer set. Then the body is pulled down so the shackle springs free. The skill is fine, multi-turn rotary control of a small real dial on a free-hanging body, with re-grasps.
setup: Metres; x forward from the line through the arm bases, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top; arm bases at (0, +0.305) and (0, -0.305). (1) Locker door section, fixed: the lock area of a single-tier steel locker door, 1 mm painted steel face with 25 mm side returns, 300 mm wide (y -0.210 to +0.090) and 250 mm tall, its face at x 0.2545 facing the robot, standing on a 90 mm steel foot behind it, clamped to the table. Hasp: a 3 mm steel tab welded square to the face in the vertical plane y = -0.060, sticking out 25 mm toward the robot (x 0.2295 to 0.2545), 22 mm tall (z 0.183 to 0.205), with a 10 mm hole (axis along y) centred 15 mm out from the face, its bottom at z 0.189. (2) Padlock, hanging, free: a 1-7/8 in (48 mm) dial combination padlock of the Master Lock No. 1500 type: stainless-steel-covered body 48 mm wide (y), 19 mm thick (x), 50 mm tall; hardened steel shackle 7 mm diameter, 19 mm inside clearance, 21 mm inside width; black dial 33 mm across standing 7 mm proud, knurled rim, 40 marks (0-39, 9 degrees apart), white index mark on the body above the dial; 163 g. Its shackle's top bar passes through the hasp hole (long leg on the -y side); it hangs under its own weight with the shackle's inside top on the hole's bottom: body centre (0.2395, -0.060, 0.145), dial centre (0.2265, -0.060, 0.145), dial facing the robot (-x). Locked, with the pack cleared by the reset: dial spun left at least three full turns and stopped at 0 (every wheel picked up to the left, so the first number needs the full right turns). Inside: a working three-gate pack on the dial axis (drive cam on the dial carrying gate 3; wheels 2 and 1 driven through 2 mm pins, so each wheel is picked up after about 319 degrees of free play), and a spring-loaded shackle (1.5 N up) held by a 45-degree ramped catch on its short leg. The catch's bolt (4.9 N spring) carries a fence that can enter the wheel rims only when all three gates (14.7 degrees wide, radial sides) are under it, i.e. each within 4 degrees of its set position, less than half a mark: a stop one mark off on any number keeps it out; then a pull of about 3 N beyond the lock's weight releases the shackle, which springs up 12 mm. Dial drag 0.008 N m, each wheel 0.002 N m. Steel on steel friction 0.3. Nothing else is on the table. Both arms start at their ready pose with the grippers open. The full dimension and mechanism table is in the README.
scoring: Read every 50 ms step from the lock's joint angles and pose and the grippers' joint states; in a real trial from a close video of the dial with its numbers legible and a photo at the end. Right means clockwise seen from the robot. Gate set = that wheel's gate within half a mark (4.5 degrees) of the fence, i.e. the dial was stopped on the number itself, not between it and a neighbour (the maker's directions say stop on each number); the fence itself reaches release depth only when all three are within 4.0 degrees, so a stop one mark off on any number leaves the lock shut. Credit counts where the gates are, however they got there; in practice only the maker's rule puts them there: (1) right, past at least two full turns, to 24 sets wheel 1; (2) left one full turn past 24 to 8 sets wheel 2 (overshooting 8, or turning right by a full turn, moves the wheels off their gates); (3) right, less than one turn, to 31 sets the cam. The start position does not count: the reset leaves the pack cleared to the left, so turning right straight to 24 sets nothing. Open = the shackle at least 8 mm up from closed relative to the body (short leg out of the body). Score at the end of the run: 1.0 the shackle open, the lock still on the hasp (the shackle's top bar within 12 mm of the hole centre), each gripper's centre point at least 30 mm from the lock's bounding box, and the lock at rest: over the last 1 s, released and on the hasp throughout, its body centre within a 5 mm box and its tilt within 5 degrees (a small leftover sway on the hasp is allowed; a lock being moved is not); 0.75 all three gates set (unlocked but not opened), or opened but still held, moving or lifted off the hasp without falling; 0.5 wheels 1 and 2 set; 0.25 wheel 1 set; 0 otherwise. Zero for the rest of the run: the lock body more than 35 mm below where it hung (fallen off the hasp), or the shackle coming open while any gate is more than one mark off (forced; judged as it opens, since the open lock's dial turns freely). A pull with a wrong combination moves the shackle under 2 mm and is not penalised. Success = 1.0 held 1 s. Real trial: a camera 150 mm from the lock, 40 degrees to the side of the gripper's line, keeps the dial numbers and index legible past the gripper; from its video, each stop's number and turning direction, by the rule above, give wheels 1 and 2; each stop counts only if the index sits on the number to within half a mark. For 0.75, at the end the judge pulls the body down by hand: it opens only if all three gates are set. The last second of video shows the lock at rest; the end photo shows the open shackle on the hasp and the grippers 30 mm clear.
run_limit: 5,000 steps (250 s at 20 Hz); the scripted demo succeeds at about step 1,980 (99 s), so the limit is about 2.5x the demo
reset_notes: Close the shackle, spin the dial LEFT at least three full turns and stop at 0 (clears the pack to a known state; the simulation's reset restores the same wheel angles), hang the lock on the hasp with the long leg on the -y side and the dial facing the robot, let it settle; return both arms to the ready pose.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz physics. The wheel pack is a simplified working pack (cam and 2 wheels, 2 mm drive pins, one fence on a sliding bolt with a 45-degree catch) sized to fit the body, not the maker's parts; its gates admit the fence within 4 degrees (half a mark is 4.5); real locks are reported to forgive more. Dial drag, springs and the ~3 N pull are estimates. Numbers aren't drawn (zero mark, index). The open shackle doesn't swivel. The locker is a door section.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (run on the earlier gate geometry with a 4,000-step limit; it moved toward the lock but never turned the dial); demo: 1.0 (success at step 1,978; each gate within 0.6 degrees of the fence when pulled)
